UsageSnapshot.swift:70 (`maxUtilization`) passes it on unchanged, VendorViewModel.swift:235/276 writes it to history, VendorViewModel.swift:150-155 reloads it within the 24h window, and SparklineView.swift:46/116/126 calls Int(...rounded()) without clamping. So a value of 1e300 would reach the trap. What fails is the claimed source. The only way to inject that value is a JSON usage response from the vendor's own API: Anthropic, OpenAI, or xAI over HTTPS to a fixed host. Kimi/Gemini base_url is host-allowlisted (AppConfig.swift:432-446), and PinningDelegate.swift:50-56 never accepts a certificate the system rejects. In the default deploy, the only parties who can write that response are the vendor itself or a MITM holding a CA trusted by the system. Both are outside the threat model, and neither is an attacker who can reach this code. The other route is the history JSONL file. That needs local write access as the same user, which already means full control of that user account. The 'One attacker-controlled usage response' precondition is assumed, never shown. What remains is a robustness bug: a missing clamp on vendor data. It is not an attacker-reachable vulnerability. OpenRouter already clamps with min(...,100) at OpenRouterWireTypes.swift:150; Anthropic, XAI and OpenAI do not.
